speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: TABLING OF INTERIM CANADA-U.S. AGREEMENT ON DUTY RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to table three copies of an interim agreement between Canada and the United States relating to rates of duty, signed today at Geneva. This agreement embodies the results of negotiations between representatives of the two countries during the multilateral tariff conference which opened at Geneva in September, 1960, under the auspices of the general agreement on tariffs and trade.
In recent years the value of the two way trade between Canada and the United States represented by the items contained in the two schedules to the interim agreement has been about $130 million to $140 million per annum. All of the items in the United States schedule provide for reductions in rate, and they apply to Canadian exports which averaged about $65 million in the three year period 1958-60. The Canadian schedule provides for reductions in duties applying to imports from the United States averaging about $63 million per annum in the same three year period. In addition, Canada bound existing free entry provisions relating to a considerable number of farm implements and other items of production equipment which had not previously been bound, and for which import statistics are not separately available.
In addition to this agreement with Canada, the United States has entered into similar agreements with several other contracting parties to the GATT, including Britain, the European economic community, Japan, Sweden, Austria, Denmark, Finland, Israel, New Zealand, Norway, Pakistan, Peru, Portugal and Switzerland.
Indirect benefits of very considerable significance to Canadian exporters will accrue to Canada under the operation of the most favoured nation principle by virtue of these interim agreements between the United States and some of the third countries I have just listed.
The multilateral effect of these agreements between Canada and the United States and between the United States and third countries will be to open greatly enhanced prospects 26207-1-99
for Canadian exports. Reduction in duties arising from this series of agreements will provide benefits to almost every sector of the Canadian economy.
The interim agreement tabled today relates to the bilateral tariff negotiations between Canada and the United States under the so-called "Dillon round" of the multilateral tariff conference at Geneva. The results of Canada's bilateral negotiations with countries other than the United States, some of which are not yet concluded, will be announced in due course and will appear as part of the official conference protocols.
The interim agreement between Canada and the United States takes effect as of the date of signature. The textual part of the agreement as tabled is in English and in French, as is the schedule of tariff concessions granted by Canada.
The schedules setting forth concessions received and granted by Canada will enter into force 30 days after exchange of notification between the two countries or at a date to be agreed upon, and will later be incorporated into the official conference protocols which cannot be issued at Geneva until the conclusion of the series of bilateral negotiations. On issuance of the conference protocols the interim agreement will cease to have force or effect.
I now table a further document which summarizes in English and in French the two schedules to the interim agreement. Hon. members will find in the summary of concessions received by Canada under the agreement three figures in brackets. The first is the duty levied at present by the United States; the second is the duty leviable after the first stage of the reduction; the third is the duty finally leviable, that is, the fully reduced rate.
The reductions in United States rates resulting from the negotiations will, almost without exception, come into force by two annual stages, the first such reduction resulting in what is described in the U.S.A. schedule as the "intermediate" rate, and the second as the "final". Precise information is not yet available as to the exact date or dates on which the President of the United States will, by proclamation, bring the reduced rates into force.
Full details of the benefits accruing to Canada under the most favoured nation principle from the series of bilateral agreements

Tabling of Agreement
between, the United States and third countries will be made public when the provisions of the numerous schedules of concessions to these agreements have been analysed.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that in relation to the coming into effect of these mutual tariff reductions hon. members are aware that the governor in council possesses power under section 10 of the Customs Tariff to make such reductions in duties on goods imported into Canada from any other country or countries as may be deemed reasonable by way of compensation for concessions granted by any such country or countries. It will therefore be open to the government to bring these reductions in the Canadian tariff into effect on the date to be agreed upon following exercise by the President of the United States of the powers conferred on him by congress under existing legislation in that regard.

We are, of course, in the position that we will have to study the minister's announcement with great care before we will be able to express our opinion as to the eventual benefits or otherwise that our country will derive.
I was a little surprised at the bias toward bilateral agreements in the announcement by the minister. I noticed that he made reference to multilateral advantages that might be derived as a result of the agreement. We were very interested in a Reuters news dispatch today emanating from Geneva to the effect that the United States has arrived at a sweeping agreement with the European common market. No one in the middle of winter, especially a Canadian winter, likes to be caught outdoors in the nude. We are hoping that it is the intention of the government to follow through and do as the United States government has done, and reach a mutually beneficial agreement with the European common market at a very early date.

subtopic: TABLING OF REPORT OF CANADA-U.S. COMMITTEE ON MIGRATORY BIRDS

speakeroldname: Hon. W. G. Dinsdale (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: TABLING OF REPORT OF CANADA-U.S. COMMITTEE ON MIGRATORY BIRDS
speechtext:
Last May my colleague the Minister of Agriculture and I met with United States Secretary of Agriculture Freeman and Secretary of the Interior Udall in Ottawa to discuss various agricultural and renewable resource problems affecting Canada and the United States. Discussions included the possibility of joint action to deal with the declining migratory water fowl population, particularly the ducks and geese, which use the international flyways.
A committee with members from each country was appointed to consider the problem. Since last May this international migratory bird committee has met twice in Washington and once in Ottawa. At the request of the committee, the United States fish and wildlife service and the Canadian wildlife service

have undertaken special studies to provide information basic to the committee's deliberations.
The committee has prepared an interim report which I wish to table at this time for the information of hon. members. The report contains several specific recommendations for action, involving pilot projects in the multiple purpose use of lands for the maintenance of water fowl population.

subtopic: DISCUSSIONS ON INDIAN AFFAIRS COMMITTEE REPORT
DISCUSSIONS ON INDIAN AFFAIRS COMMITTEE REPORT
speechtext:
Have the recommendations of the joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons on Indian affairs presented to the house on July 8, 1961, been discussed with any interested parties other than members of the cabinet and civil servants: and, if so, what is (a) the name and address of each such party (b) the date or dates upon which each discussion took place (c) the opinion of each such party (d) the action contemplated with respect thereto?
Answer by: Mrs. Fairclough:
(a) and (b). Discussions of a purely informal nature have been held, in the course of regular departmental business, with various individuals and groups across the country. These have involved numerous individual officers of the Indian affairs branch and interested persons outside the department and it would not be practical to attempt to list them in detail. However, among the major organizations who have either made representations or discussed various aspects of the recommendations informally with departmental officers, or considered them at annual meetings, are the Indian association of Alberta, the federation of Saskatchewan Indians and the Indian-Eskimo association of Canada. In addition, the recommendations of the joint committee were discussed fully at the Indian superintendents' national conference held in British Columbia in 1961.
(c) and (d). It is not possible at this stage to state the opinion of the parties or groups concerned, since the discussions were of a purely exploratory nature. Nor is it possible

speechtext: I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Public Works. I was able to notify his office this morning of my intention to ask this question. speakeroldname: Hon. D. J. Walker (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REDUCE DANGER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is the department's practice to open all the French river dams as soon as possible at the close of the navigation season to permit the emptying of

the lake prior to the coming spring freshet. This has been done; the lake level is already below the recognized "empty" elevation of 638.0, and it would appear that we may be able to lower it still further to possibly elevation 637.5.
The water content of the snow cover on the watershed is about 10 per cent greater than normal, and all dams are still fully opened. These will remain opened as long as possible.
It is too early to make a firm forecast on the magnitude of the coming spring freshet. The general picture is, however, not too reassuring at this time. Much will depend upon the amount of snowfall still to come, the duration of the break-up and the amount of spring rainfall. While we expect a heavy run-off, the course of events of the next three weeks can alter our forecast considerably. Our reasons for expecting a heavy run-off are the higher than average water content of the snow cover and the lack of a pre-spring thaw this year.
Our officials are also in close communication with officials of Ontario hydro and of the Ontario department of lands and forests, who have storage dams on the rivers emptying into the lake, and up to date information on the condition of the watershed is known at all times.

There is one thing I should like to have cleared up. While this thought has not been communicated to me by people who have borrowed under this act, the same thought has been asked of me by fishermen with respect to loans under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. The principle is the same. Perhaps if I ask the question of the minister now, the answer will be equally applicable to both acts.
During the resolution stage, the minister indicated that this was the fifth or sixth extension of this particular act and that the extension contemplated now is for a three year period from July 1 of this year to the end of June, 1965. I have been unable to answer the question asked of me, except to say that past experience has shown that extensions are put into effect as the expiry date approaches. However, this does leave some doubt in the minds of individuals who are contemplating borrowing money under this legislation, and I am sure it may leave some doubt in the minds of lenders as to their position following the expiration of this piece of legislation. I realize that this procedure permits a review of the legislation every two or three years instead of dealing with the matter during consideration of the estimates.
I wonder whether or not any thought has been given, and undoubtedly it has, to placing legislation of this sort on a more permanent basis. I realize that once you put things of this nature into effect, especially when the legislation is renewed five or six times before the expiry date, you establish a practice and thus put the act on some kind of permanent basis. I just want to pose this question: Has consideration been given to a more equitable way of dealing with legislation of this nature, that is giving it a more permanent basis, rather than having the possibility of its cancellation become a reality every two or three years?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO GUARANTEE LOANS, ESTABLISH LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext:
I think hon. members will appreciate at once that parliament can make this legislation permanent if it

chooses to do so. This would, however, immediately raise the question of the permissible aggregate of the guarantees. It has accorded thus far with the views of parliament that legislation of this kind should be given a three year life. This method assures parliamentary control and discussion of the legislation every three years, and thus the establishment of an appropriate ceiling on loans being made for the ensuing three year period.
Now, if we are to change the whole scheme of the act and withdraw the expiry date of the legislation, that would immediately present a problem as to what should be established as the aggregate or ceiling in perpetuity. I think hon. members will appreciate that this would not accord with the established conception of parliamentary control.
In so far as the position of borrowers or lenders under this legislation is concerned, the expiry date has no effect whatever on the validity of obligations incurred under the terms of the act before the expiry date. Even if the legislation expired at the next expiry date, it would have no bearing whatever upon the valdidity of obligations incurred or undertaken under the provisions of the act prior to that date. There is, therefore, no difficulty whatever about borrowers or lenders entering into their transactions under the terms of the legislation in that regard. The three year life does not deter any borrower or any lender under the act for that reason.

I appreciate the latter part of the minister's remarks to the effect that, even if the act expired, the loans would continue in effect and the guarantees would continue in effect, although the force of the legislation would be gone in so far as new loans were concerned. It seems to me that there was one year in which the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act almost expired before an extension was granted. When the matter reaches this stage, I know fishermen have expressed the view to me that they feel they rush into doing contemplated work in order to participate in these loans and make sure they are able to borrow money before the legislation expires. If they had some degree of assurance the legislation was going to be extended, then they could plan their borrowings more easily so that they would fit into the economics of the industry.
These are views I have had expressed to me. As I said, the only answer I could make, and perhaps I will have to continue to make it, is that so long as the present Minister of Finance is minister he is too nice a fellow to cancel this legislation out. You can rest assured from past experience he will introduce a measure before parliament to secure an extension. However, I have to qualify this by

saying that I have heard some doubts expressed as to whether or not he will be minister when this legislation is under review in 1965, regardless of the fortunes of his party. I doubt very much whether he is going to be in that position in 1965 when this legislation is reviewed.

I should like to reiterate what I said on a previous occasion and ask the minister, once again, to consider altering another section of the act, perhaps even at this time, by unanimous consent, or by a subsequent amendment later this session.
The section to which I refer is the section of the act which we discussed last evening, and I am asking the minister to consider an amendment raising the limit on permitted loans from the present statutory ceiling of $4,000 to at least double that amount. The figure of $8,000 has been suggested by the united fishermen and allied workers' union to the minister and others, and I assume that would be a reasonable ceiling to have. In the bill the house has just dealt with, the ceiling there has been increased from $3,000 to $7,500, I believe, and the same principle applies to the act which the bill now before us seeks to amend.
Despite what the minister said last night, fishermen have told me they do not make plans to enter extensively upon repairs, acquisitions or alterations by borrowing under the terms of this act because they know the present limit is set at $4,000. Even though

the minister told us last night that there is no pressure on the present ceiling-and I do not doubt for one moment that this is what the lenders have said-I submit that if this is the position it is primarily because fishermen do not go to the banks asking for, say, $6,000 only to discover at that point that the permissible loan cannot exceed $4,000. Of course, they generally know this beforehand, and in connection with this act they do not plan on the basis of borrowing more than $4,000. Consequently we find that the average amount lent is considerably below $4,000. I think hon. members will find that a considerable proportion of the borrowings are in respect of such things as radio telephones or depth sounding equipment, or for repairs to engines, or new engines-something of that sort, all of which would cost less than $4,000. It is when you get into the field of buying a boat or buying a share in a fishing boat that you exceed the $4,000 limit. As I said last night, $4,000 would not even buy a gill-netter, and a gill-netter is a one-man boat used for fishing salmon on the British Columbia coast. That is, generally, the lowest cost vessel which a man can buy, and a good gill-netter costs in the neighbourhood of $8,000 anyway. When it comes to trollers and seiners we find that the cost is far in excess of $4,000. I do not presume to apply my remarks to the Atlantic provinces, because different circumstances prevail there-there are different methods of fishing, different species of fish and the like-but as far as the west coast is concerned I am sure the minister will find that an amendment of the kind I have suggested will help the fishermen to take advantage of the principle of this act and enable them to borrow sufficient money to enhance their position in the industry.
We placed on record last night correspondence and resolutions in this regard. We know the minister is aware of these things. I think it would not be good enough to wait until 1965, when this legislation might be further extended, before getting around to considering whether or not the limit on the loan should be raised. I feel sure that if the minister were desirous of taking action along the lines I have suggested we could hold up this legislation and find some way of putting the suggested change into practice. The rules are intricate and I do not know whether raising the limit from $4,000 to $8,000 would constitute another money bill and thus require a resolution stage, or whether, now that we are in committee following a resolution stage, we could take the action I suggest without further delay. I have some doubts about that.
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act
Perhaps the minister could at least give us an indication that this question will be given serious study. In 1959 he said the question would be given serious study, that it would be discussed with those concerned. Last night he said nobody had told him about it; nobody had brought this matter to his attention since the last time it was discussed. We showed that the minister was not accurate in this regard. However, if the hon. gentleman can indicate that this is a matter about which he is really concerned, if he would consult with his colleague the Minister of Fisheries, who knows at first hand the effects of this legislation, I am sure the committee would be satisfied. The fishermen concerned would certainly be satisfied to obtain from the minister some indication that this matter was being seriously studied. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources tells us he has files labelled "For active consideration". Perhaps the Minister of Finance could open a couple of files under the same heading and give the fishermen an opportunity of participating fully in the benefits of this act, as the original legislation of 1955 intended them to. This would go a long way toward making them feel happier about this measure. I do not say they are unhappy about the provisions which exist at the moment or about the extension which is proposed here. I speak of those who are able to borrow under the terms of this act. However, those who are not able to borrow- and they include the majority of fishermen- are not happy about the fact that they are not able to prosecute the fishery to the fullest possible extent because of the limitation placed on the loans which may be made to them.
I therefore appeal again to the minister to indicate that this matter is being given sympathetic or active consideration and that he hopes to introduce legislation on a subsequent occasion, perhaps next session or even this session, to remedy the situation. I urge the minister to ask unanimous consent to amend the act again, which would be most helpful to the people concerned.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in 1962 the railway industry of North America is at a time of complete reappraisal. The Americans are the latest into the field with a presidential report which goes into the question of operating costs, particularly of railway labour. But there are ramifications of that report which suggest that one of the main troubles and difficulties of United States railways is the question of consolidation of lines.
Recently in Canada we have had the long, long hearings of the royal commission on transportation and after a considerable time a two volume report which in essence, it seems to me, has a message for us that we should be vigilant and very deliberate in our scrutiny of any extensions of railway service in this country, particularly the building of new lines. I think hon. members who have read volume 2 of the report of the royal commission-I know that members from the west will be conscious of this because there has been considerable reaction on the prairies -will agree that the main advice of the royal commission is that the railways, particularly in western Canada, be allowed to get out of the operation of unremunerative branch lines as much and as quickly as possible. The theme of the report of the royal commission on transportation is surely that we must be extremely critical of any extension of lines unless there is a tremendous, almost bona fide case of a prosperous service, and I mean prosperous not only to the region concerned but to the railway.
In recent months a two volume history of the Canadian National Railways has been
1578	HOUSE OF
Canadian National Railways issued which in some ways makes interesting reading to go along with the two volume report of the royal commission on transportation. This two volume history by Colonel Stevens sets out a long and almost terrifying record of mismanagement on the part of the railway builders of this country. You are left with the impression, after reading the two volumes, that generations to come as well as this generation will be paying for the tremendous over optimism connected with the construction of railway lines. Certainly, it makes interesting reading to put Colonel Stevens' report in juxtaposition to the report of the royal commission on transportation which underlines again and again the need to make the railways more competitive. One of the ways to do this is to get the railways out of a situation in which they cannot possibly get a reasonable return on their investment.
I give this preamble, Mr. Chairman, because some of the evidence that was revealed before the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines would seem to indicate that this proposed line has a rather shaky economic basis. In order to make the point, Mr. Chairman, I want to touch on some of the evidence that was revealed. I think the first point one should acknowledge in relation to this is that the conception the minister and the government are bringing forward in connection with the extension of this line along the south shore of the St. Lawrence is a fine one in that it is conceived as being a means of improving a section of the country that has been passed by in the general economic growth. In this sense, it is impossible to criticize the intention of the bill. We support that intention and anything that will help the more backward parts of the country, in an economic sense.
When we come to look at the arrangement that has been made, the expenditures that are going to be made, and the facilities that now exist, very grave doubts about the whole project come to our mind. I think the first point that has to be very clear is that the Canadian National Railways would have no part of this enterprise on its own. In other words, the Canadian National Railways would not take this project and make it their own.
I am sure this proposal must have been made to them at some time or other and they turned it down. Therefore, the government had to come up with the proposal that they would provide the money for the construction of the line, they would look after the debt side of it and the Canadian National would merely be the builders and operators. There would be a separate fiscal division. This is the first 

thing we need to know about this project. It seems to me that Canadian National, in its considered judgment, turned this line down on an economic basis. I believe that is a fair statement, and I do not think the minister would disagree with it.
The next point it seems to me that we need to look at is the facilities that already exist in this particular region. As has been noted, this region is not like the area that is going to be served by the Pine Point railway or some of the other railways that are being built, such as the Chibougamau road to the north. This railway will be an extension into an area that has been settled for a long time and into which there are highways. It is a general area in which there is some rail traffic on the south, but this is not so from Matane to Ste. Anne des Monts. It is an area with a traffic-carrying complex built into it in the form of roads, water carrier services and other associated means.
It has been the experience of most of us who have looked at the development of railways, that railways cannot compete in so far as passenger traffic and high revenue freight traffic are concerned where there are roads established and where the haul is relatively short. This is one of the reasons, as most members know, that the Canadian Pacific and Canadian National have gone in so heavily for trucking. It is because they cannot by rail alone really cover this very remunerative field of high revenue traffic. In this particular region, we have these services already provided through the truckers and through the highways that now exist. The main reason railways are built today, and the minister brought this point up in committee as did his advisor, Mr. Scott, is that railways are carriers of bulk tonnage at very low cost. This is the main reason railway lines are built today. Almost invariably they are tied in with the sort of contract mentioned in committee, Mr. Chairman. We had problems in our own area connected with bulk contracts for the shipment of iron ore.
I was in Montreal this morning, Mr. Chairman, to see how the negotiations were going, between the iron mines and Canadian National Railways in our own part of the country. The Canadian National is insistent that it will not give any easement in the rate that they are now putting into effect for this-iron ore unless they have some guarantee of tonnage. This is something they regret very much not getting years ago when they originally entered into the provision of ore dock facilities and other things for the ore mines at Atikokan. This point needs to be-underlined.

The minister says the railway is ideally designed for bulk traffic of the low revenue kind, at least that low revenue traffic is involved. Here is a situation where several million tons are being carried and the railway is trying to nail down the mine to even higher incentive figures.
I refer hon. members to the evidence which came out in committee. The estimated tonnage given to us by Mr. Scott, the economic adviser to the minister, was 75,000 tons of outbound traffic and 65,000 tons of inbound traffic. The revenue on inbound traffic would be $2 a ton and for outbound traffic $1.50 a ton, which gives approximately $240,000 of estimated operating revenue. This $240,000, Mr. Chairman, is set against, as near as we can judge it, a capital expenditure of $14 million.
Now, this is almost fantastic when we realize the operating revenue in sight. Of course, this is only the first year, and according to the minister the traffic future would be much brighter after that. What evidence did the minister give us in regard to the expansion of traffic? He told us that there would be a possibility of more pulpwood being shipped. I can paraphrase the evidence given by the adviser to the minister, and I do not think it is unfair, that the railway line would mean more suitable cutting in the area. He pointed out that there would be more even depletion rather than so much emphasis on the western end, and I suppose he was referring to the western end of Gaspe. What a purpose for a railway. Any information one can gather about the pulp and paper industry, Mr. Chairman, has led me to believe that it is generally agreed that shipping by log boom tends to be cheaper than by any other means, provided it does not cost too much to provide the waterways and flumes. In this particular case with the location of the mills across on the north shore at Baie Comeau, and at Gaspesia Paper in southern Gaspe, and the mills in Quebec city and Three Rivers, because of distance there is not much chance of booming pulpwood from the Gaspe to these mills. But there can be water movement by barge. It is cheaper to move pulp by barge or some kind of ship movement during the very long summer season in that area, rather than by truck or rail.
At the present time out of Matane into Quebec city and the Three Rivers area there is only a movement of 50,000 cords, and I wonder if hon. members realize how small
50,000	cords are. In northwestern Ontario, which is not much more populated than Gaspe, we have a cut of 2.5 million cords and that cut gets to the mills in various ways.
Canadian National Railways The point there is that the cut through Matane is only 50,000 cords at the present time.
We might favour the proposal more if the minister could come and tell us that his officials of the C.N.R. had been to any of the pulp and paper companies and they had given any indication of the volume that was going to be secured of pulpwood haul on the railway. There is no evidence of that whatsoever and even Mr. Dingle indicated that the C.N.R. had not bothered to talk to anybody about this as yet.
The minister's economic advisors came up with a figure of 25,000 tons, possibly rising to
35,000	tons, of wood chips to be transported on the railway; but I would point out to hon. members what a pittance this really is. It will barely keep the average size mill going for 15 or 20 days in the year and it certainly is not an economic basis on which to build large bulk, small revenue traffic for a new branch line. Furthermore there is no suggestion by the economic advisors that this pulp rail haul to the Quebec area could be at a price which would be economically feasible, and there is no indication that the pulp and paper companies are really interested in it.
The only indication presented by the minister and his advisor to our committee was that one corporation, the St. Lawrence corporation, had indicated a volume of wood chips that might be shipped out from the Gaspe area in association with the waste from the saw mill enterprises, but no indication was given of where there might be a possibility of bulk traffic that would bring something to the railway in terms of bulk pulpwood. The minister says that the cut is 50,000 cords, but even 200,000 cords is a pittance in terms of revenue as a haul from Ste. Anne des Monts to Quebec city or Three Rivers.
The argument in so far as the pulp and paper industry is concerned really does not stand up to close examination. It must be taken into consideration that the crown lands in this area are held by a number of large paper pulp corporations, and smaller lots are held by small contractors. When we look at this particular situation we have no pattern to indicate where any attempt is going to be made to consolidate these holdings. We have no indication that the government and the railway have got together with the provincial government that controls these crown lands to say "maybe we should build a pulp mill on the north shore of Gaspe". Yet the government is prepared to put $14 million into this particular line.
That shows an economic faith that I find almost unbelievable, but let us turn to the

Canadian National Railways other part of wood production where there is an indication of some kind of volume shipment. That is the indication that at the present time in the Gaspe area there are 75 saw mills with a capacity of 85 million board feet per year. Now I accept the fact that the building of this line will enable some of this wood, but not all of it, to compete more effectively in the Montreal market, but we are given no indication as to the relative amount of this wood which comes by water from the Gaspe area.
The minister further has indicated that he is going to improve the ports, including the port at Ste. Anne des Monts. How does he know when he improves it that it will not be a more effective means of providing cheaper transportation for the lumber from Gaspe into the Quebec and Montreal city areas? It is usually the case that water shipment is cheaper than rail for a bulk commodity such as raw lumber, or even dressed lumber, and it must be remembered that the port facilities at Montreal and Quebec city have distribution facilities. Therefore it is hard to see where, in respect of a product such as lumber, one which really has some large substance on the market at the present time, it is going to gain so tremendously from a railway line 57 miles long.
The situation in so far as products of the forest, particularly pulpwood, are concerned is not a very attractive one and we have no indication of a real economic survey or any real research having been done by the minister's department with regard to future prospects in this particular regard. In effect we are given a number of pious statements, and all I can say with regard to these pious hopes in so far as forest industries are concerned is that I come from an area which depends for its real life blood upon the products of the forest-and this is an area where the railway lines have been paid for a long time ago-these railway lines cannot compete with other forms of transportation.
Over the last 10 years we have been seeing a revolution in transportation in the woods, and this applies to other commodities as well, where an increasing emphasis has been placed on trucking. Now the Gaspe area has trucks and highways, so again we begin to wonder about the whole story of this $14 million expenditure for a railway line that apparently the minister's economic advisors cannot really indicate has any substance in its immediate future. When I say "immediate future" I am thinking in terms of five or 10 years, because to create a pulp and paper mill usually takes five or 10 years. To create the kind of operation that would make it economical to


ship wood and paper pulp by this rail project would probably take much longer than five years.
The other will-o'-the-wisp, beacon, or siren that the minister put forward to justify the building of this line is the fact that there are large mineral deposits lying just to the south of Ste. Anne des Monts, an area to which this line will go. Why is it that in almost all the other railroad projects we have heard about in recent years, when a mine wants a railway the railways are willing to put in the line? We struck a hot base metal find in our area at Geco and we got two railway lines there.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED PROCEDURE TO PROVIDE COMPENSATION FOR CROP FAILURES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of providing comprehensive income payments to farmers in time of crop failure by giving consideration to amending the Prairie Farm Assistance Act so as to provide: (a) an increase in the schedule of payments as follows: (i) an increase in the maximum payment from $4 per acre to $8 per acre; (ii) an increase in the present $3 per acre payment to $6 per acre; (iii) an increase in the present $2 per acre payment to $4 per acre: (b) an increase in farmers' contributions from 1 per cent to 2 per cent; (c) an increase in the maximum cultivated acreage on which payments may be made from 400 acres to 600 acres; and should give consideration to the provision of other appropriate amendments required to assure adequate income support in time of crop failure.
He said: I am pleased at this time to move this resolution for the consideration of the house. It is designed to extend the scope of an act which has been on the statute books of this country for a long time. I refer to the

Prairie Farm Assistance Act which was placed on the statute books for the first time in 1939. This act has been of great benefit to farmers in western Canada during years of crop failure.
It is an act to which farmers themselves as well as the federal treasury make a contribution. Over the years, payments of approximately 50 per cent have been made by the producers and 50 per cent by the federal treasury. This act has been improved from time to time over the years. When it was first placed on the statute books it required an area in Saskatchewan with a crop failure in some 135 townships, or 100 townships in Alberta or Manitoba before payments could be made. Since that time the area has been reduced, and now the basic unit for the operation of the act is one township. This means that in any year when there is a crop failure in any real sense the act becomes operative, and while it does not work on an individual basis-while there is still a great measure of rough justice in its administration -nevertheless the vast majority of producers who experience crop failure do receive some benefit under the legislation.
To sum up the purpose of this resolution in a nutshell, it is to double the benefits and double the contributions. The wording in the last section of the act "400 acres to 200 acres" would probably better be spelled out by saying "one half of 200 acres up to 600 acres". Of course, half of 400 acres is the basis on which the wording is put into the act. This act, over the years, has cost the federal treasury a good deal of money. It is estimated that over the last 21 years the total benefits paid out have been in the neighbourhood of $261 million until this year, and the farmers have paid $127 million of that amount. This means that year in and year out the federal government has, on an average, contributed some $6 million.
The proposals in this resolution, if they were implemented, would mean an additional burden on the treasury of perhaps $6 million to $10 million a year over a long period of time and would double the contributions made by the producers under this act.
The Prairie Farm Assistance Act was brought into this house by the late Hon. J. G. Gardiner and it is one of those acts which he fostered and which he supported. He was able to amend it in a beneficial way from time to time. It has stood the test of time. It is a good act, and what I say in favour of this act today I have said on many occasions in the past. All I am saying now is that the time has come when there should be further improvements made to a very good act.
Prairie Farm Assistance Act
We have a crop insurance scheme which deals with the same general field of crop failure. The present Crop Insurance Act has many shortcomings in my opinion. When it was before this house I criticized the fact that the federal government was prepared to assume only 20 per cent of the estimated premium cost over a period of years, that the federal government was not prepared to assume any part of the losses themselves, and that if there were a series of serious losses under the Crop Insurance Act the provincial treasuries would become bankrupt. I contend that the Crop Insurance Act as it has been placed before this house is not a substitute for the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and that the Crop Insurance Act has been found wanting in many respects. It is used rather extensively in the province of Manitoba. It has been used in a very limited way in Saskatchewan. It has not been used at all in the province of Alberta.
The province of Saskatchewan, so I understand, is prepared this year to continue the operation of the Crop Insurance Act in co-operation with the federal government but in order to protect the provincial treasury the provincial authorities are saying that they are prepared to pay losses only to the extent of $5,000. This very seriously limits the application of the crop insurance scheme in that province. I asked the Prime Minister a few days ago whether there had been in consultation between the federal government and provincial governments with respect to providing a system of reinsurance so that the provincial treasuries would be protected in times of severe crop failure, particularly while the fund was being built up. The answer given by the Prime Minister was that no consultations had been held between the governments-there had merely been individual contacts between officials of the federal department and the provincial departments. I submit that this is not good enough. I submit that the federal government has failed to take the lead in encouraging the operation of a crop insurance scheme adequate to protect the farmers of western Canada. I submit that the government has promoted in this country a crop insurance scheme which is largely impracticable, one which is largely inoperative and which does very little to protect western producers. If the federal government would pay a sum larger than 20 per cent, if the federal government would take the initiative in bringing about a method by which there would be co-operation in reinsurance between the federal government and the provinces, then the crop insurance plan might have a much

Prairie Farm Assistance Act greater application and be of much greater benefit. But until that is done, the crop insurance scheme will be of very limited value.
The last time the Prairie Farm Assistance Act was amended to increase the total payments under the act was in 1957. Up until that time the maximum payment a farmer could receive was $500, or $2.50 an acre on one half of 400 acres. Now the maximum is a total of $800, or $4 per acre on one half of 400 acres. I am asking by this motion that the maximum of $4 an acre be made $8 an acre, that the payment of $3 an acre for a yield category of from three to five bushels be made $6 an acre and that the $2 an acre payment of from zero to three bushels be made $4 an acre. This would be a straight doubling of the payments within this yield category.
The further proposal is that in recognition of the general increase in the size of farms since 1939 the government should consider an increase in the acreage on which benefits may be paid and that it should consider a 50 per cent increase in the acreage on which benefits could be paid. This would mean for a larger farm-and perhaps I should call this an average size farm because there are a great many farmers today who have up to 600 cultivated acres-a maximum payment in the lowest yield category of $2,400.
I have in my hand the August 1961 issue of the Economic Annalist which gives the 11-factor cost of production index. This index shows tremendous changes in the farmer's costs of production over the years. In 1939 the index stood at $99.3. In April of 1961 the index had risen to $283.4. In other words from 1939 to 1961 the cost of production index has almost tripled.
The maximum payment under the act in 1939 for the smaller acreage or the acreage then provided was $500. For a similar acreage under the proposal I am placing before the house today the maximum payment would be $1,600. That is very close to the change in the cost of production and would merely mean that for a farm of this size in 1962 the farmer would be able to receive a sum of money with approximately the same purchasing power as the dollar had in 1939.
I realize that there are certain areas of western Canada where prairie farm assistance has very little appeal. I realize there are areas of western Canada where this proposal will not receive wide support. However, it is my experience that taking western Canada as a whole over the years P.F.A.A. has been very acceptable, has received the support of western farm organizations and I am led to believe the proposal I now have before the house would receive similar support.
[Mr. Argued

As to the future I think we should develop a better P.F.A.A. It may be advisable also to develop a more adequate Crop Insurance Act. It may be that at some time in the future these two acts can meet so that together they will give the western farmer some protection in time of crop failure.
The kind of measure I propose today is not something that is a cure-all for the problems of western Canada. It would merely mean that in time of widespread crop failure there shall be a basic minimum below which the farmer's income will not be allowed to drop. This basic minimum income for a farm of 400 cultivated acres in time of total disaster would be $1,600, which I submit is not a tremendous sum of money with costs as high as they now are. I suggest that the cost of a measure of this kind can be borne quite readily by the federal treasury. When you compare the cost of this kind of legislation with the $1 an acre payment, provision for which was recently made, or the payment of storage costs, provision for which has been on the statute books for a long time, the cost of this type of provision cannot be regarded as prohibitive in any sense.
The Prime Minister said in the throne speech that certain payments would be made to farmers who have suffered from crop failure. Those payments have not been made to farmers who suffered crop failure but to all farmers. In keeping with the sentiments expressed in the Prime Minister's statement I suggest this kind of provision should be given favourable consideration by the house, that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act placed on the statute books in 1939 has proved of great value, that its benefits should be increased and that the farmers themselves are willing to pay more into the act if they are allowed to receive greater benefits.

speechtext:
It would be interesting to the house to have the viewpoint of the Liberal party because hon. members in the official opposition have been going through Quebec saying that the western farmers do not need any additional support and do not need acreage payments. How does the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska feel about this motion. This matter is of very great interest to me as my constituency has always been one of those in Alberta which have benefited a great deal from P.F.A.A. While I realize this fact, I must point out that my constituency is in the unique position of having half of it benefit a great deal from P.F.A.A. and the other half benefit very little
Prairie Farm Assistance Act at all. Hence I hear two sides of the story as I go throughout the east central part of Alberta. I hear those who would like more money under P.F.A.A. and I hear those who would like to do away with it altogether. It would be interesting to hear what the other members of the newly found party of the hon. member for Assiniboia have to say on this matter. My mind is taken back to the time when this question was raised in the house in 1958. At that time the hon. member for Assiniboia was going throughout the country saying that the Conservative party has 47 members from western Canada but that it would take them four years to find out where to hang their hats. May I say that it has taken him 17 years, Mr. Speaker, to find out where to hang his hat; and we who formerly came from Saskatchewan are not sure that in 17 more years he will not be hanging it somewhere else.
This is a question on which one must gauge the remarks emanating from the Liberal party having regard to where they come from; I refer to the new, the old, the this and the that. This is a question that I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, all members of the house should take into consideration when they study this resolution. Certainly the constituency of the hon. member for Assiniboia will benefit perhaps to some extent by this resolution if no further changes were made with regard to P.F.A.A. When he mentioned this matter in the house in 1958 I asked him to what rate he would then raise the percentage in P.F.A.A. He said he would triple it. I observe that he has now reduced the figure to 2 per cent instead of 3 per cent. Maybe this is the effect of the switchover. I do not know. I will leave it to him to decide. However, this is the change that he has talked about.
There is another thing I should like to point out to the rest of the house. He has mentioned that this would perhaps just double everything in the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. It would also double the contributions made by the federal government towards western Canada. This is a point in which the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska would be quite interested in view of the remarks he has been making throughout his home province with regard to western farmers.
Actually from 1939 until 1959 something like $101 million were paid into the prairie farm assistance fund through the 1 per cent levy on farmers, and $202 million were paid out under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Those are approximate figures. Hence the federal government has stood practically half the cost. I also think it fair that it be pointed out here that Saskatchewan has been the big

Prairie Farm Assistance Act beneficiary. They have been receiving something like $2 for every $1 they put into it, Alberta about $1.50 and Manitoba were lucky if they broke even. Perhaps that is why crop insurance has gone over so well in that province. However, in doubling the contributions as suggested in this resolution the farmers would then be paying approximately, on the average, $20 million every year into P.F.A.A. The federal government, of course, would perhaps be paying out, on the average, $40 million every year. When you consider the $40 million every year and the crops raised on the acreage, this comes to something very close to 6 per cent. This 6 per cent under the Manitoba crop insurance plan will get you a better return than the $8 an acre suggested here by the hon. member for Assiniboia. While I and a great many of my constituents would benefit by this proposal, I think it only fair that some of these things be pointed out to the house and to both parties.
Another thing that should be pointed out is this. The hon. member for Assiniboia suggested that some day in the future the Crop Insurance Act and the Prairie Farm Assistance Act may meet. I suggest that they meet right now if the province will get a move on and do something about the matter. Manitoba has taken quite a large forward step, in my opinion, in offering the farmers crop insurance, that is in areas in which the P.F.A.A. does not cover the situation too well because of the minimum they must have in order to qualify, because of poor crop below 8 bushels an acre. Half townships are obliged to qualify.
The hon. member for Assiniboia never mentioned today the question of individual basis. Actually more farmers are concerned with receiving P.F.A.A. or crop insurance on an individual basis. He failed to mention that matter in his talk. I think this will be a far better step; I refer to bringing it down on an individual basis. It would do away with any conflicting crop reports turned in by one farmer and another. Actually I realize that bringing it down on an individual basis would be difficult under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act as it now stands. But under the Crop Insurance Act there is no real difficulty in this matter. In fact, most of the crop insurance is written up, as I understand it, on an individual basis.
This points out one of the advantages a farmer can have by taking out crop insurance or advocating, as is the case in Alberta, that the provincial government devise a crop insurance scheme. Another advantage is this and I point it out purely to show the house the differences between the two pieces of legislation. In the P.F.A.A. the payments


cover a limited number of acres. In this motion I think the hon. member has suggested that the number be increased from 400 acres to 600 acres. Here again he is catering perhaps to some of the larger farmers. Maybe he has all the large farmers in Saskatchewan down in his area.

We in Acadia appreciate the P.F.A.A. It has done a great deal for my constituency and we wish it to continue to give service to that area. Actually I point this out because of the number of farmers I meet in the north and northwestern part of my constituency who have failed to benefit even in the last few years. Since 1958, when we amended the act, 15 per cent to 20 per cent more farmers are qualified under the P.F.A.A. than were qualifying previously. This takes in all those persons who have side incomes such as that from perhaps a part-time job on a railway or in an army camp or in a small town and are farming on the side. They can now collect under P.F.A.A. An elevator man or a school teacher who is farming on the side can now collect under P.F.A.A. When this change was made in 1958 it allowed something like 15 to 20 per cent more people to qualify for assistance. While the formula of 50 per cent paid by the farmer and 50 per cent paid by the federal government has been true in the past, I question whether or not it will remain true in the future because of the greater number of people qualifying under

the Prairie Farm Assistance Act today. I believe I have pointed out to the house some of the difficulties and possible results that this resolution might have and I think that it requires considerable study.

I wish to say a few words on this resolution sponsored by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). I am in agreement with the intention of the hon. member to provide farmers with sufficient income with which to pay operating expenses in years of crop failure due to drought, or other cases over which the farmer

has no control. However, the P.F.A.A. was implemented in the thirties as a measure of relief to enable the farmer and his family to live. The provincial government and municipalities assisted the farmer with the purchase of feed and seed grains on a loan basis until the farmer could get a crop which would enable him to repay his loan. This legislation has been amended from time to time to enable more farmers to qualify, by reducing the area and increasing the compensation.
In 1958, the act was amended to remove many of the inequities in the making of payments and to broaden the coverage. The result has been from 10 to 15 per cent more farmers benefit from this legislation than previously benefited from it. This whole matter of income for farmers has been of great concern to this government. In order to stabilize the income of farmers, particularly in years of crop loss, this government in July, 1959, passed the Crop Insurance Act. It was hoped this would enable farmers to help themselves and would meet conditions such as were experienced during this past season.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to put on the record the regulations which are necessary to enable farmers to benefit from this worth-while legislation, as many hon. members may not be familiar with it. This legislation has been of great benefit to the farmers in Manitoba who have carried crop insurance. I quote:
The act provides that Canada will pay 50 per cent of the administrative costs of any insurance scheme plus 20 per cent of the premiums paid in any year. The contribution of 20 per cent of the premiums is similar to that paid by Canada to the unemployment insurance fund.
In addition, Canada may in any year loan to a province up to 75 per cent of the amount by which indemnities exceed premium income plus reserves plus $200,000.
There is no compulsory feature in crop insurance but the agreements now in force provide that at least 25 per cent of the farmers in any area covered by the insurance scheme must participate before the scheme can operate.
The coverage provided under any agreement with a province shall not exceed the established value of 60 per cent of the long term average yield. The established value of each crop is determined by any method agreed on by Canada and the provinces. The long term average yield of an insured crop in any area is calculated and determined in a manner approved by the federal Department of Agriculture. In the Manitoba agreement the long term average yield is calculated over a 35 year period. However, different periods of time may be used depending largely on yield records which are available.
It is generally accepted that the 60 per cent coverage provided is approximately equal to the cash cost of production.
Just what are the costs of production in Manitoba? The hon. member for Assiniboia has said that under his plan of amending the P.F.A.A., the farmer could collect $1,600.
Prairie Farm Assistance Act I have been advised that in Manitoba some of those farmers who carried crop insurance collected over $5,000. Surely, this is a scheme that would be approved by any farmer who wanted coverage which would enable him to pay the expenses connected with farming. Now, the rates which applied in Manitoba are simply these, as it states here:
The premium rates between townships in the northwestern area from 61 to 10 per cent (or 98 cents to $1.51 per acre) for a coverage of-

It is taken off their cheques when they take their grain to the elevators. That is the trouble. Possibly your party did not have strong enough representation, and I sympathize with your efforts over the past four years in that you did not understand the problem in western Canada. This resolution is not a new one. We discussed it the first year we were down here and some of the western members representing the foothill constituencies said "our farmers won't go for it". The constituency represented by the hon. member for Acadia, and my own, have benefited more from this act than any other constituencies in Canada, and I would point out it was never intended to be an insurance act. By its name it is an assistance act and if this resolution goes through it will be a means of putting the

farmers back to where they were in the 1930's. They would have to look to the municipalities for relief.
In the first place the payments under this act were never meant to cover all the losses in production. They were just intended to be of assistance and they are not given to the landowner himself. They are actually given to the operator of a farm, the one who has to put in the crop the following year, and it is not a matter of covering his complete losses.
I have made mention of spring wheat areas and they can be divided into two parts, the part known as the prairies or great plains, and the part known as woodland and parkland. Climatic conditions in each of these areas vary from year to year. We in the prairies or great plains area suffer from drought, frost, rust, hail and so on, and in the long term average over a period of 45 years one would think we should have given up farming on this type of land. However, over a 45 year period on that type of land we have had an average production as great as if not greater than the parkland area, and I think it is in the interests of the people of Canada to keep that group of farmers on that land to produce more crops of wheat.
Agriculture used to be first in our exports. Now it is third and we must maintain our production on the western prairies.
I should like to say something about how this program is financed. Farmers contribute to the program to the extent of 1 per cent of their sales of wheat, oats, barley, rye, flax and rapeseed. The last two were included last year and all farmers are covered in the program. When I mention "farmers" I mean
